# topic: Chapter 13: The Old South, 1820-1860
# title: HIS-201 Ch. 13 — 3 Numbers & Dates
# short: 3 Numbers & Dates
# order: 3
# expect: 22
How much of the world's cotton the United States produced by 1860
column2: By 1860 the United States produced three-fourths, or 75 percent, of the world's cotton.

column1: How far west cotton had spread by the Civil War
column2: By the eve of the Civil War, nearly a third of the total cotton crop came from west of the Mississippi River.

column1: How many enslaved people the Upper South sold to the Deep South
column2: Slaveholders in the Upper South sold 2 million Black men, women, and children to planters in the Deep South, a trade that separated one-fifth of husbands and wives there and one-third of all children from their parents.

column1: What a prime field hand could cost in the late 1850s
column2: A prime field hand could sell for up to $1,500 in the late 1850s.

column1: How rural and unindustrialized the South remained in 1860
column2: In 1860, 84 percent of the South's labor force was engaged in farming, compared with 40 percent in the North, and the South produced only 9 percent of the nation's manufactured goods.

column1: How urban the South was compared with the North in 1860
column2: Only 1 in 10 southerners lived in cities and towns in 1860, compared with 1 out of 3 in the North, and New Orleans, with 169,000 people, was the only truly southern city of significant size.

column1: How limited southern schooling and literacy were
column2: Southern white children spent about one-fifth as much time in school as northern children, and 20 percent of native-born southern whites were illiterate, compared with 3 percent in the middle states and 0.4 percent in New England.

column1: When slavery ceased to be a national institution
column2: In 1776 slavery had been a national institution, but by 1820 it was confined to the states south of Pennsylvania and the Ohio River.

column1: Where the slave population was most concentrated by the 1850s
column2: More than half of enslaved people lived in the Deep South, African Americans outnumbered whites in South Carolina and Mississippi by the 1850s, and in the Upper South only Virginia and North Carolina had a slave population above 30 percent.

column1: What share of white southerners belonged to slaveowning and planter families in 1860
column2: Of 8 million white southerners in 1860, only about 2 million, or one-quarter, belonged to slaveowning families, and only about 1 out of every 30 belonged to families of the planter class that owned 20 or more slaves.

column1: How wealth was distributed among planters
column2: About 10,000 families owned 50 or more slaves, about 2,000 owned 100 or more, and the planter class owned more than half of all slaves and more than 90 percent of the wealth; a typical plantation had 20 to 50 slaves and 800 to 1,000 acres.

column1: The South's 1860 population mix
column2: The 1860 southern population was about 12 million, roughly two-thirds white, one-third enslaved, and about 2 percent free Blacks.

column1: How common poor whites and landowning yeomen were
column2: Yeomen made up more than half the southern white population, about 80 percent of them owned their land, usually 80 to 160 acres, and poor whites were only about 5 percent of the white population.

column1: How long slaves worked at peak season
column2: During cultivation and harvest, slaves were in the field 15 to 16 hours a day, from just before sunrise until dusk, with work uncommon on Sundays and often only a half day required on Saturdays.

column1: The usual weekly slave ration
column2: Each adult could expect about a peck of cornmeal, 3 or 4 pounds of bacon or salt pork, and molasses, a monotonous fare of almost 5,400 calories that still lacked several essential nutrients.

column1: When Gabriel's Rebellion and Denmark Vesey's conspiracy occurred
column2: Gabriel Prosser's planned march on Richmond took place in 1800, and Denmark Vesey's Charleston conspiracy was crushed in 1822.

column1: When Nat Turner's revolt occurred, and how many whites it killed
column2: In 1831, after an eclipse of the sun, Nat Turner and six confederates began the revolt, gained some 70 recruits, and killed 57 white men, women, and children.

column1: How many enslaved husbands and wives the domestic trade separated
column2: From 1820 to 1860 more than 2 million slaves were sold in the domestic slave trade, and such sales separated perhaps 600,000 husbands and wives.

column1: How many southern African Americans were free in 1860
column2: Of the 4 million African Americans living in the South in 1860, only 260,000, about 7 percent, were free, more than 85 percent of them in the Upper South, with almost 200,000 in Maryland, Virginia, and North Carolina alone.

column1: When the Virginia Debate took place, and how it ended
column2: The Virginia legislature debated the future of slavery from January 16 to 25, 1832, then refused to act by a vote of 73 to 58, the last significant attempt of white southerners to challenge the peculiar institution.

column1: When Calhoun called slavery a "positive good"
column2: In 1837 John C. Calhoun declared slavery a "positive good," part of the closing of white southern ranks after 1831.

column1: How much of the South was still uncultivated in 1860
column2: As late as 1860, 80 percent of the region remained uncultivated, even as single-crop agriculture wore out soils and wheat plowing intensified erosion in the Upper South.
